title: Conservation of Momentum
short_intro: The law of conservation of momentum states that the total linear momentum of an isolated system of interacting particles remains constant in time. It is a fundamental conservation law directly linked to the homogeneity of space, as articulated by Noether's theorem.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Application of linear momentum conservation in one and two-dimensional collisions, recoil of guns, and direct central impacts.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Variable mass systems (rocket propulsion), generalized momentum in Lagrangian mechanics, system of particles with central forces, and relativistic momentum.

concept_notes.heading: Law of Conservation of Linear Momentum
bullets: If the vector sum of external forces acting on a system is zero, the total linear momentum of the system remains conserved.
Mathematically expressed as dp/dt = F_ext; therefore, when F_ext = 0, p = constant.
It holds true for macroscopic as well as microscopic systems, independent of the nature of internal forces (whether conservative or non-conservative).

concept_notes.heading: Internal vs External Forces
bullets: Internal forces are forces exerted by particles of the system on one another, which always occur in action-reaction pairs according to Newton's third law.
By Newton's third law, the vector sum of all internal forces within a closed system is identically zero.
Only external forces from outside the system can alter the total linear momentum of the system.

concept_notes.heading: Momentum Conservation in Collisions
bullets: During collisions, impulsive internal forces are extremely large compared to external forces, making external forces negligible during the impact duration.
Thus, total momentum is strictly conserved immediately before, during, and immediately after any collision.
Collisions are categorized into elastic (kinetic energy conserved) and inelastic (kinetic energy not conserved), but momentum is conserved in both types.

concept_notes.heading: Application to Variable Mass Systems (Rocket Propulsion)
bullets: For systems like rockets where mass changes due to fuel consumption, the system must include both the rocket and the ejected exhaust gas.
The instantaneous thrust force on the rocket is given by the product of the relative exhaust velocity and the rate of mass ejection.
Conservation of momentum allows integration of velocity changes over time to yield Tsiolkovsky's rocket equation.

derivations.title: Conservation of Momentum from Newton's Second Law
derivations.conditions: System of n interacting particles with zero net external force.
steps: Let the total momentum of the system be P = sum(p_i) = sum(m_i v_i).
The time rate of change of total momentum is dP/dt = sum(dp_i/dt) = sum(F_i).
The total force F_i on the i-th particle includes external force F_i^(ext) and internal forces F_ij from other particles.
By Newton's third law, internal forces cancel out in pairs since F_ij = -F_ji.
Therefore, dP/dt = sum(F_i^(ext)). If the net external force is zero, dP/dt = 0, which yields P = constant.

derivations.title: Tsiolkovsky Rocket Equation
derivations.conditions: Vertical or free-space motion of a rocket in the absence of external drag and gravitational forces.
steps: At time t, mass of the rocket is m and velocity is v. Momentum is p(t) = mv.
In time interval dt, mass decreases by dm (dm is negative) and exhaust is ejected with relative velocity v_rel.
At time t + dt, rocket mass is m + dm and velocity is v + dv, while ejected mass dm has velocity v - v_rel.
Equating total momentum at t and t + dt: mv = (m + dm)(v + dv) + dm(v - v_rel).
Expanding and dropping second-order small terms (dm dv), we get m dv = -v_rel dm.
Integrating from initial mass m_0 to m and initial velocity v_0 to v yields the final velocity expression.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Force vs Time Graph during Collision
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A bell-shaped curve plotting impulsive force F(t) on the y-axis against time t on the x-axis.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: The area under the force-time curve represents the linear impulse delivered to the body, which equals the total change in linear momentum.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested numerically to find momentum change from graphical areas or average force calculations.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Linear Momentum vs Time for an Isolated System
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A straight horizontal line parallel to the time axis indicating constant total momentum.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Since no external force acts on the isolated system (F_ext = 0), the rate of change of momentum is zero.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Conceptual identification questions in TGT/PGT examinations regarding isolated vs non-isolated systems.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Ballistic Pendulum Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic of a bullet of mass m embedding into a suspended wooden block of mass M, causing a vertical rise h.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Combines momentum conservation during the instantaneous collision with mechanical energy conservation during the subsequent swing.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Standard apparatus-based problem solving for finding bullet velocity.

solved_numericals.question: A shell of mass 20 kg moving with a velocity of 10 m/s explodes into two fragments of masses 5 kg and 15 kg. If the 5 kg fragment comes to rest, find the velocity of the 15 kg fragment.
solution_steps: Initial momentum of the shell: P_i = M * u = 20 kg * 10 m/s = 200 kg m/s.
Let the velocity of the 15 kg fragment be v. Mass m_1 = 5 kg with v_1 = 0 m/s, mass m_2 = 15 kg with velocity v.
By conservation of momentum: P_i = m_1 * v_1 + m_2 * v.

solved_numericals.question: A rocket has an initial mass of 1000 kg (including 800 kg fuel). It ejects gas at a constant relative velocity of 2000 m/s and at a fuel consumption rate of 10 kg/s. Find the thrust force and the acceleration of the rocket at the start of its motion (neglect gravity).
solution_steps: Thrust force formula: F_thrust = v_rel * (dm/dt) = 2000 m/s * 10 kg/s = 20000 N.
Initial mass of the rocket m_0 = 1000 kg.
Acceleration at the start: a = F_thrust / m_0 = 20000 N / 1000 kg = 20 m/s^2.

solved_numericals.question: A ball of mass 0.5 kg moving at 6 m/s strikes a smooth vertical wall normally and bounces back with the same speed of 6 m/s. What is the magnitude of the impulse delivered by the wall to the ball?
solution_steps: Choose direction away from the wall as positive. Initial velocity u = -6 m/s, final velocity v = +6 m/s.
Impulse J equals change in momentum: Delta p = m(v - u).

assumptions_and_limitations: Conservation of linear momentum applies strictly in inertial frames of reference unless pseudo-forces are explicitly introduced in non-inertial frames.
At relativistic speeds (v comparable to c), classical momentum p = mv must be replaced by relativistic momentum p = m_0 v / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2).

common_misconceptions.wrong: Internal forces can change the total momentum of a system if the bodies have different masses.
common_misconceptions.correct: Internal forces can never change the total momentum of a system.
common_misconceptions.why: By Newton's third law, internal forces occur in equal and opposite pairs, canceling out completely for the system as a whole.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Kinetic energy is always conserved whenever momentum is conserved.
common_misconceptions.correct: Momentum is conserved in inelastic collisions, but kinetic energy is not.
common_misconceptions.why: Kinetic energy can be transformed into heat, sound, or deformation energy during interactions, whereas momentum remains invariant in the absence of external forces.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Momentum conservation depends on the type of forces (conservative or non-conservative) acting internally.
common_misconceptions.correct: Momentum conservation depends only on the absence of net external forces.
common_misconceptions.why: Internal conservative and non-conservative forces both satisfy Newton's third law pairs of action and reaction.

quick_revision: Total linear momentum is conserved if and only if the net external force acting on the system is zero.
Linear Momentum Definition: p = m v
Newton's Second Law in Momentum Form: F_{ext} = \frac{dp}{dt}
